quote: 20.1 Vendor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Customer, its Affiliates, and their directors, officers, employees, and agents from each third-party claim and resulting damages, settlements, judgments, penalties, costs, and reasonable attorneys' fees arising from an allegation that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate an intellectual property right.
rationale: Section 20 meets the preferred position. Vendor defends and indemnifies Customer and its Affiliates for third-party IP infringement/misappropriation claims (20.1) and for Vendor's breach of Applicable Law, bodily injury/property damage, unauthorised access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor, and Vendor's gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud (20.2). Standard procedure (prompt notice, cooperation at indemnitor's expense, control of defence, no prejudicial settlement without consent) appears at 20.4, and 20.5 provides the procure/modify/replace/refund remedies without cutting off the defence obligation. Customer's reciprocal indemnity at 20.3 is appropriately narrow (unmodified Customer-supplied material used strictly as authorised, and Customer's violation of Applicable Law), with carve-outs for Vendor Technology, modifications and combinations. Indemnification obligations are Excluded Claims under 21.3, so the Vendor indemnity is not subject to the general liability cap — better than the fallback super-cap. No redline required.

verification.notes: No proposal: element-level redline verification is not applicable.

quote: 14.2 Upon creation and subject to payment of the applicable Fees, Customer owns each Deliverable created specifically for Customer. Vendor hereby assigns to Customer all worldwide right, title, and interest in those Deliverables and shall obtain equivalent assignments from its personnel.
rationale: The IP package meets our preferred position. Section 14.1 confirms Customer owns all Customer Data, Customer-provided material and independently developed IP, with only a limited processing right to Vendor for service delivery, reinforced by Section 15.1 (no sale, advertising use, data combination or model training without our consent). Section 14.2 vests ownership of Deliverables in Customer with an express Vendor assignment, personnel assignments and further-assurance obligations. Section 14.3 leaves Vendor with its pre-existing Vendor Technology but applies the Section 13.2 perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid licence (including rights to modify and create derivative works) to any Vendor Technology embedded in a Deliverable, and requires pre-delivery identification of such material. Section 14.4 excludes joint ownership absent a signed instrument setting out exploitation rights, and feedback is voluntary with no assignment of Customer rights. Nothing elsewhere assigns our IP or data to Vendor.
ruleTitle: Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data

quote: 24.1 Customer may assign this Agreement or an Order Form without Vendor's consent to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger, reorganization, acquisition, or sale of all or substantially all assets or business to which the Agreement relates.
rationale: Section 24 sits at our preferred position. Customer may assign to an Affiliate or M&A successor without Vendor consent (24.1, notice only); Vendor may not assign, delegate material performance, or transfer by change of control without our consent (not unreasonably withheld) and never to a Customer competitor (24.2); other assignments are subject to a mutual reasonableness consent standard (24.3); and 24.4 expressly bars any Vendor right to terminate, suspend, reprice, accelerate Fees, or reduce service on our change of control. Cross-check of Section 9 termination triggers shows no change-of-control or assignment-based Vendor termination right (9.2 covers insolvency only and expressly excludes a lawful reorganization that does not impair performance), and Section 13.4 confirms licence rights transfer with a Section 24 permitted assignment. No redline required.

quote: Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment.
rationale: No exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation binds Customer anywhere in the Agreement. Clause 12.3 affirmatively preserves our freedom to develop, acquire or license any product or service and to engage any supplier, and expressly records that Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, MFC, minimum-volume or no-hire commitment; clause 2.1 confirms there is no minimum quantity or purchase commitment and that declining to place further Order Forms is not a breach. The only exclusivity-flavoured restriction (clause 12.4, barring Vendor from marketing a directly competing analytics service) runs against Vendor and benefits us, so it is not flagged. This meets the preferred position.

Clause 12.3 expressly confirms the preferred position: Customer remains free to develop, acquire, license, sell or use any product or service, engage any supplier, and operate in any field or territory, with Vendor acknowledging that no exclusivity or non-compete commitment has been made. The only competition-related covenant, clause 12.4, binds Vendor (it may not develop or market a service competing with Customer's analytics products during the term), which benefits our party and is not flagged. quote: 9.4 Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form without cause by delivering the written notice specified in Section 29.4. Customer owes only accrued Fees, and Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees for the period after termination.
rationale: Section 9.4 gives Customer an unrestricted termination-for-convenience right over the Agreement or any Order Form, with the notice period fixed at thirty days by Section 29.4, liability limited to accrued Fees (no early-termination fee or penalty), and a refund of prepaid Fees for the post-termination period (reinforced by Section 10.2). Sections 9.1-9.3 give Vendor only for-cause and insolvency termination rights, and no Vendor convenience or mid-term walk-away right appears anywhere in the document (Section 24.4 expressly denies one on change of control). This matches the preferred position, so no redline is warranted.

quote: 22.1 Vendor may audit Customer's compliance with licence quantities no more than once in any twelve-month period, on at least thirty days' prior written notice, during normal business hours, and in a manner that does not unreasonably disrupt Customer. An audit will be conducted off-site where practicable by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality.
rationale: Section 22 is the only audit right binding us and it meets the preferred position on every material term: frequency capped at once per twelve months, thirty days' prior written notice, normal business hours, off-site where practicable, independent auditor bound by confidentiality, Vendor bears cost unless underpayment exceeds five percent, and express prohibition on direct access to Customer systems, unrelated Customer Data, privileged material and third-party confidential information. Section 22.3 adds customer-favourable protections (findings are our Confidential Information, use limited to enforcement, copy of report, and finality of the audited quantity on payment). No remote-access or unannounced audit language appears elsewhere in the document. No redline required.

quote: 28.1 This Agreement and each dispute arising from it are governed by the laws of the State of New York, without regard to conflict-of-law principles.
rationale: The clause sits at our preferred position: New York law governs (with CISG expressly disclaimed), and the state and federal courts in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction with irrevocable submission and waiver of forum objections. quote: 21.1 Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the Fees paid or payable by Customer under the first Order Form during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: The cap is mutual, indirect damages are mutually excluded (21.2), the Excluded Claims carve-outs in 21.3 cover confidentiality, data protection/security, indemnities, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement, and Customer's payment obligation is expressly not "damages" — all at or above the preferred position. The quantum, however, is illusory: "Fees" is defined (1.5) as the Implementation Fee, which is "the one-time implementation charge of USD 12,000 stated in the first Order Form" (1.8), and 21.1 further limits the basis to the first Order Form. The effective cap is therefore about USD 12,000 regardless of subscription spend — far below 12 months' fees and below even 6 months' charges, which is walk-away territory. Minimal fix: rebase 21.1 on all amounts paid or payable under the Agreement and all Order Forms in the preceding 12 months, with the USD 1,000,000 floor; no other part of Section 21 is touched.

verification.notes: Operation 1 completes the preferred cap with a minimal operator/number substitution: it correctly rebases limb (a) on "fees paid or payable in the 12 months preceding the claim" (removing the illusory "Fees ... under the first Order Form" anchor) and adds the USD 1,000,000 limb as a greater-of. All preferred carve-outs and the mutual consequential-damages exclusion were already present in 21.2–21.3 and were left untouched. Operation 2 was unnecessary: the existing sentence ("Customer's obligation to pay undisputed Fees for conforming Services is not damages") already satisfied the preferred element that Customer payment obligations are not damages, so no edit was needed to complete the selected level. Operation 2 also worsens our position by deleting the "undisputed" and "for conforming Services" qualifiers, exposing Customer to uncapped liability for disputed amounts and amounts invoiced for non-conforming Services — an unrelated commercial protection that should have remained effective. Note only in the rationale: limb (a) now uses lowercase "fees" rather than the defined term "Fees", which is deliberate (the definition is the USD 12,000 implementation charge) but should be flagged so it is not later conformed back to the defined term.

quote: 7.6 Vendor warrants that Fees charged to Customer will be no less favourable than fees offered to any similarly situated customer for comparable volumes and terms.
rationale: The sole most-favoured-nation provision (§ 7.6) is granted by Vendor in our favour: Vendor warrants that Fees charged to Customer will be no less favourable than those offered to similarly situated customers. Nothing in the fee provisions (§ 7), Order Form terms (§ 4), or General (§ 30) obliges Customer to extend best terms to Vendor or to match third-party offers, and there is no exclusivity or right-of-first-refusal construct that operates as a customer-side MFN. This meets the preferred position (no MFN obligation on Customer, Vendor-granted MFN welcome), so no redline is proposed.

Section 7.1 reinforces this by barring any unstated minimum-use or similar charge, and Section 12 records that we have made no minimum-volume or exclusivity commitment. Sections 4 and 8 contain no committed volumes: Order Forms renew for twelve-month periods but we may opt out on thirty days' notice (with a reminder-backstop), and the audit shortfall language in Section 22 is a true-up of audited quantities, not a take-or-pay penalty. No redline needed.

rationale: Section 19 meets the preferred position. Vendor warrants Services will be performed in a professional and workmanlike manner by qualified personnel to industry standards (19.1); Deliverables materially conform to documentation and acceptance criteria for ninety days after delivery or acceptance, whichever is later, and Hosted Services conform throughout the subscription term — better than a fixed 12-month software period (19.2). Compliance with Applicable Law and a no-malicious-code warranty are included (19.3). The remedy is real: prompt re-performance, repair or replacement, with termination and refund of Fees paid if Vendor cannot cure, and it is expressly non-exclusive for fraud, infringement, confidentiality, privacy, security and indemnified claims (19.4). The disclaimer in 19.5 is mutual, limited to implied warranties, and expressly does not limit any express warranty, service level, indemnity or remedy, so it does not swallow the express warranty. Nothing to redline; Section 6 acceptance and Section 3 service levels are addressed under their own rules.

quote: 7.7 If any invoice is not paid within ten days of its due date, Customer shall pay Vendor, as liquidated damages and not as a penalty, an amount equal to fifteen percent of the annual Fees for each week the invoice remains unpaid.
rationale: Section 7.7 imposes liquidated damages payable by Customer to Vendor at fifteen percent of annual Fees for each week an invoice is late, triggered by a ten-day payment delay. That is directly contrary to the preferred position (no liquidated damages or penalties payable by Customer) and is not saved by the fallback, which permits only a capped early-termination fee. Because the charge compounds weekly without any cap and is triggered by a minor and potentially inadvertent delay, it sits in walk-away territory (it can quickly exceed the remaining contract value and is unenforceable as a penalty in substance despite the label). Nothing else in the Agreement caps it: Section 21.3 confirms payment obligations are outside the liability cap. We have proposed replacing it with customary late-payment interest on undisputed overdue invoices, which reaches the preferred position with a minimal edit while leaving Vendor a proportionate remedy. Service credits or SLA remedies running to Customer are unaffected.

verification.notes: Preferred level is complete: the operative words now provide that Customer pays no liquidated damages and no penalty for late invoices, deleting the fifteen percent weekly charge. The added catch-all "and no amount in the nature of either" duplicates the protection already given by "no liquidated damages and no penalty" and is more than needed to reach the preferred position; deleting the payment obligation (or flipping the two operative nouns) suffices. The retained trailing words "for each week the invoice remains unpaid" leave a slightly awkward residue attached to a nil obligation, but they create no contradiction and Vendor's other non-payment remedies elsewhere remain effective. Fallback is separate and unmet, which is irrelevant because the locked target is preferred.
